The Dixiecrats, formally the States' Rights Democratic Party. They were Southern Democrats who split from the national Democratic Party in 1948 to oppose President Truman's civil rights initiatives.

The party formed after Harry Truman desegregated the military and endorsed a federal civil rights agenda. The Southern Democratic establishment viewed these policies as a betrayal. Strom Thurmond, a South Carolina segregationist, won the party's presidential nomination. He carried Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and South Carolina—the only five of the Solid South states to break Democratic ranks in that election.

The Dixiecrats won 2.4 percent of the popular vote and 39 electoral votes, the strongest third-party electoral showing since the Bull Moose Party in 1912. Their platform defended racial segregation as constitutionally legitimate under the Tenth Amendment and opposed federal intervention in Southern social and racial affairs.

Though the Dixiecrats themselves dissolved after 1948, the movement's constituency—white Southern voters—gradually migrated to the Republican Party over the following decades. This process, accelerated during the 1960s and beyond, was accelerated by what became known as the Southern Strategy. The Dixiecrat defection was the first crack in the Solid South, a Democratic bastion that had endured since Reconstruction. It foreshadowed the Republican takeover of the South by the 1980s, fundamentally reshaping American electoral politics and the geography of party power.
